slides.definition: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, networking, and management of containerized applications.
slides.why_it_matters: Modern applications require automated deployment, self-healing, scaling, and consistent runtime environments across cloud and on-premise systems.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company runs 200 microservices. Kubernetes automatically restarts failed containers, distributes workloads, and scales services based on demand.

architecture_flow.diagram: User → kubectl → API Server → Scheduler → Worker Node → Pod → Container Runtime

core_concepts.name: Declarative Management
core_concepts.definition: User defines desired state and Kubernetes continuously works to achieve it.
core_concepts.usage: Used with YAML manifests through kubectl apply.

core_concepts.name: Cluster
core_concepts.definition: A group of machines running Kubernetes workloads.

core_concepts.name: Control Plane
core_concepts.definition: Components responsible for managing cluster state.

comparisons.summary: Containers share the host kernel and are lightweight, while VMs include full guest operating systems.
Imperative defines actions; declarative defines the desired final state.

error_symptoms.impact: Applications cannot be deployed or managed

resolution_prevention.best_practice: Always define desired state using manifests.

response: Kubernetes manages containerized applications by maintaining the desired state.
It provides deployment, scaling, networking, and recovery automation.
interview_answer.why: Interviewers expect understanding beyond definition.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Kubernetes is not a container runtime; it orchestrates containers using a control loop model.

dynamic_cards.content: Most Kubernetes problems are caused by incorrect desired state, networking, or resources.

slides.definition: Kubernetes cluster architecture consists of Control Plane components that manage the cluster and Worker Nodes that run application workloads.
slides.why_it_matters: Understanding architecture helps troubleshoot failures, design production clusters, and answer system design interview questions.
slides.real_world_scenario: A production cluster has three control plane nodes and multiple worker nodes. If a worker fails, Kubernetes reschedules workloads automatically.

architecture_flow.diagram: kubectl → API Server → etcd → Scheduler → kubelet → containerd → Container

core_concepts.name: API Server
core_concepts.usage: All cluster operations go through API Server.

core_concepts.name: etcd
core_concepts.definition: Distributed key-value database storing cluster state.

core_concepts.name: Scheduler
core_concepts.definition: Assigns Pods to suitable Worker Nodes.

core_concepts.name: Controller Manager
core_concepts.definition: Runs controllers that maintain desired state.

core_concepts.name: kubelet
core_concepts.definition: Agent running on each worker node.

comparisons.summary: Control Plane manages the cluster; Worker Nodes execute workloads.
containerd runs containers; kubelet manages Pods.

error_symptoms.impact: Pods cannot run on affected node

investigation.expected_finding: Memory pressure, network failure, kubelet errors

response: Kubernetes follows master-worker architecture.
Control Plane manages desired state while worker nodes execute workloads.
interview_answer.why: Architecture questions are common in senior interviews.

slides.interview_kill_shot: API Server is the only component that directly communicates with etcd.

dynamic_cards.content: Kubernetes controllers continuously compare desired state with actual state.

slides.definition: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes that contains one or more containers sharing network, storage, and lifecycle.
slides.why_it_matters: Most Kubernetes workloads run inside Pods. Understanding Pod behavior is essential for deployment, debugging, and production operations.
slides.real_world_scenario: A web application runs in a Pod with an application container and a logging sidecar container that ships logs to a monitoring system.

core_concepts.name: Single Container Pod
core_concepts.definition: Pod running one main application container.

core_concepts.name: Multi Container Pod
core_concepts.definition: Multiple containers sharing lifecycle and networking.

core_concepts.name: Init Container
core_concepts.definition: Container that runs before application containers start.

core_concepts.name: Sidecar Container
core_concepts.definition: Helper container running alongside main container.

core_concepts.name: Ephemeral Container
core_concepts.definition: Temporary debugging container added to running Pods.

comparisons.summary: Container runs application; Pod provides Kubernetes execution environment.
Init runs before application; Sidecar runs with application.

code_examples.title: Pod Manifest
code_examples.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx

rca.root_cause: Configuration error, dependency failure, resource issue

resolution_prevention.anti_pattern: Running unrelated applications in one Pod.

response: Pod is the smallest Kubernetes scheduling unit.
Containers inside a Pod share network namespace and volumes.
interview_answer.why: Almost every Kubernetes interview starts with Pods.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Kubernetes does not deploy containers directly; it deploys Pods.

dynamic_cards.content: Never use standalone Pods for production workloads because they do not self-heal.

slides.definition: Labels are key-value metadata attached to Kubernetes objects that help identify and organize resources. Selectors use labels to find matching objects.
slides.why_it_matters: Labels create relationships between Kubernetes resources such as Services, ReplicaSets, Deployments, and Pods.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company runs multiple versions of an application. Labels separate production, staging, and testing Pods so traffic can be routed correctly.

steps: Traffic or management actions are applied
architecture_flow.diagram: Deployment Selector → Label Match → Pod Selection → Service Routing

core_concepts.name: Labels
core_concepts.definition: Small identifying metadata attached to Kubernetes objects.

core_concepts.name: MatchLabels
core_concepts.definition: Equality-based selector matching exact key-value pairs.

core_concepts.name: MatchExpressions
core_concepts.definition: Advanced selector supporting operators like In, NotIn, Exists.

core_concepts.name: Annotations
core_concepts.definition: Metadata used for additional non-identifying information.

comparisons.summary: Labels are used for selection; annotations store descriptive metadata.
MatchLabels supports exact matching; MatchExpressions supports advanced rules.

code_examples.title: Label Selector Example
code_examples.snippet:
selector:
  matchLabels:
    app: nginx

labels:
  app: nginx

security_considerations: Avoid exposing sensitive data in labels

response: Labels connect Kubernetes resources.
Selectors determine which resources are managed or receive traffic.
interview_answer.why: Many production issues are caused by label mismatch.

slides.interview_kill_shot: A Service does not target Pods by name; it targets Pods through selectors.
follow_up_questions: How are labels used in deployments?
common_pitfalls: Changing labels of managed resources incorrectly

dynamic_cards.content: Most Kubernetes routing problems are label-selector problems.

slides.definition: ReplicaSet ensures that a specified number of Pod replicas are running at all times.
slides.why_it_matters: ReplicaSets provide availability by replacing failed Pods automatically.
slides.real_world_scenario: An application requires three instances running. If one Pod crashes, ReplicaSet creates a replacement automatically.

architecture_flow.diagram: ReplicaSet → Pod Template → Pods → Self Healing

comparisons.summary: Deployment manages ReplicaSets and provides rollout/rollback features.
Pod runs workload; ReplicaSet maintains Pod count.

resolution_prevention.best_practice: Use Deployments instead of managing ReplicaSets directly.

response: ReplicaSet maintains the required number of Pod replicas.
Deployments use ReplicaSets internally.
interview_answer.why: Shows understanding of Kubernetes workload hierarchy.

slides.interview_kill_shot: ReplicaSet answers: 'How many Pods should exist?' Deployment answers: 'How should versions change safely?'

dynamic_cards.content: Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet during every version update.

slides.definition: A Deployment is a Kubernetes workload resource that manages ReplicaSets and provides declarative updates for Pods.
slides.why_it_matters: Deployments enable zero-downtime releases, automatic rollbacks, version management, and controlled scaling.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company releases version 2.0 of an API. Kubernetes gradually replaces old Pods with new Pods while keeping traffic available.

architecture_flow.diagram: Deployment → ReplicaSet(v1) → Pods → ReplicaSet(v2) → Rolling Update

core_concepts.name: Rolling Update
core_concepts.definition: Default update strategy where old Pods are gradually replaced with new Pods.

core_concepts.name: Rollback
core_concepts.definition: Ability to revert Deployment to a previous revision.

core_concepts.name: Recreate Strategy
core_concepts.definition: Stops all existing Pods before creating new ones.
core_concepts.usage: Applications that cannot run multiple versions together.

core_concepts.name: Canary Deployment
core_concepts.definition: Releases new version to a small percentage of users first.

comparisons.summary: Deployment manages versions and rollout; ReplicaSet only maintains Pod count.
Rolling update avoids downtime; Recreate causes temporary downtime.

code_examples.title: Deployment Manifest
code_examples.snippet:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
 replicas: 3
 strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate

investigation.expected_finding: Waiting Pods or failed update reason

rca.root_cause: Bad image, configuration issue, failed health checks

resolution_prevention.best_practice: Always deploy using immutable image versions.
resolution_prevention.anti_pattern: Using latest image tag in production.

response: Deployment manages ReplicaSets and provides controlled application releases.
It supports scaling, rollback, and rolling updates.
interview_answer.why: Deployment is one of the most asked Kubernetes interview topics.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Deployment creates ReplicaSets; ReplicaSets create Pods.

dynamic_cards.content: For production releases explain Deployment + Rolling Update + Readiness Probe together.
A Deployment does not guarantee application correctness; it only maintains desired state.

slides.definition: A Service is a Kubernetes networking object that provides a stable endpoint to access a group of Pods.
slides.why_it_matters: Pods are temporary and their IP addresses change. Services provide stable networking and load balancing.
slides.real_world_scenario: A frontend application communicates with backend Pods. When backend Pods restart, the Service keeps the same endpoint and redirects traffic automatically.

core_concepts.name: ClusterIP
core_concepts.definition: Default Service type exposing application internally inside cluster.

core_concepts.name: NodePort
core_concepts.definition: Exposes Service on a port of every node.
core_concepts.usage: External access without cloud load balancer.

core_concepts.name: Endpoints
core_concepts.definition: Actual Pod IP addresses behind Service.

comparisons.summary: ClusterIP is internal; LoadBalancer exposes externally.
Service provides networking; Ingress provides HTTP routing rules.

code_examples.title: ClusterIP Service
code_examples.snippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
 type: ClusterIP
 selector:
  app: backend

resolution_prevention.best_practice: Always verify endpoints when debugging Services.

response: Service provides stable networking for dynamic Pods.
It uses selectors to identify backend Pods.
interview_answer.why: Service troubleshooting is a common production scenario.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Service does not route to containers directly; it routes to Pod endpoints.

rapid_fire_qa.question: Which component handles Service rules on nodes?

dynamic_cards.content: When Service fails, check: Selector → Endpoints → Pod readiness.

slides.definition: Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that manages external HTTP and HTTPS access to Services using routing rules.
slides.why_it_matters: Ingress provides centralized traffic management, domain-based routing, TLS termination, and reduces the need for multiple LoadBalancers.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company hosts multiple applications. api.example.com routes to backend service while web.example.com routes to frontend service using one public endpoint.

architecture_flow.diagram: User → LoadBalancer → Ingress Controller → Service → Pods

core_concepts.name: Ingress Resource
core_concepts.usage: Defines hosts, paths, and TLS settings.

core_concepts.name: Ingress Controller
core_concepts.usage: Examples include NGINX or cloud controllers.

core_concepts.name: Path Routing
core_concepts.definition: Routes traffic based on URL path.
core_concepts.usage: /api goes to backend, / goes to frontend.

comparisons.summary: Ingress provides HTTP routing; LoadBalancer only exposes a service.
Resource defines rules; controller executes them.

code_examples.title: Ingress Example
code_examples.snippet:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
spec:
 rules:
 - host: app.example.com

rca.root_cause: Wrong service name, port, or TLS config

response: Ingress manages external HTTP traffic and routes it to Services.
Ingress Controller processes those rules.
interview_answer.why: Ingress is common in production Kubernetes designs.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Ingress is not a Service replacement; it sits in front of Services.

dynamic_cards.content: Always mention Ingress Controller when explaining Ingress.

slides.definition: ConfigMap stores non-sensitive application configuration separately from container images.
slides.why_it_matters: It allows changing configuration without rebuilding application images.
slides.real_world_scenario: The same application image runs in development, staging, and production with different database URLs stored in ConfigMaps.

comparisons.summary: ConfigMap stores normal configuration; Secret stores sensitive data.

response: ConfigMaps separate configuration from application code.
interview_answer.why: Common twelve-factor application principle.

slides.interview_kill_shot: ConfigMaps are for configuration, not secrets.

slides.definition: Kubernetes Secret is an object used to store sensitive information such as passwords, tokens, certificates, and keys.
slides.why_it_matters: Applications require credentials securely without hardcoding sensitive data inside images or manifests.
slides.real_world_scenario: A backend application connects to a database using credentials stored in Kubernetes Secrets instead of plain text configuration.

core_concepts.name: Opaque Secret
core_concepts.definition: Default Secret type for arbitrary key-value data.

core_concepts.name: TLS Secret
core_concepts.definition: Secret containing TLS certificate and private key.

comparisons.summary: ConfigMap stores normal configuration; Secret stores sensitive information.
Environment exposes values as variables; volume exposes files.

response: Secrets store sensitive application data separately from code.
They can be consumed through environment variables or volumes.
interview_answer.why: Security questions frequently include Secret handling.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Base64 encoding is not encryption; protect Secrets using encryption at rest.

dynamic_cards.content: Treat Secrets as sensitive even though Kubernetes stores them as objects.

slides.definition: Kubernetes storage allows Pods to persist data beyond container lifecycle using volumes and persistent storage objects.
slides.why_it_matters: Containers are temporary. Stateful applications require reliable data storage.
slides.real_world_scenario: A database Pod restarts, but customer data remains available because it uses a PersistentVolumeClaim.

comparisons.summary: emptyDir is temporary; PV survives Pod recreation.

rca.root_cause: No matching PV or StorageClass issue

response: PV represents storage, PVC requests storage, and StorageClass automates provisioning.
interview_answer.why: Storage is important for databases and stateful workloads.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Pods consume PVCs, not PVs directly.

slides.definition: StatefulSet manages stateful applications that require stable network identity, ordered deployment, and persistent storage.
slides.why_it_matters: Applications like databases require predictable identities and storage that survives Pod recreation.
slides.real_world_scenario: A MongoDB cluster requires stable Pod names and persistent disks. StatefulSet maintains those identities.

architecture_flow.diagram: StatefulSet → Pod-0, Pod-1, Pod-2 → Persistent Volumes

core_concepts.name: Ordered Scaling
core_concepts.definition: Pods start and stop in sequence.

comparisons.summary: Deployment is for stateless apps; StatefulSet is for stateful workloads.

slides.definition: DaemonSet ensures that a copy of a Pod runs on every selected node in a Kubernetes cluster.
slides.why_it_matters: DaemonSets are used for node-level services that must run everywhere.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company deploys a log collector on every worker node to collect application logs from all containers.

architecture_flow.diagram: Cluster Nodes → DaemonSet Controller → One Pod per Node

core_concepts.name: One Pod Per Node
core_concepts.definition: DaemonSet schedules a Pod on each matching node.

core_concepts.name: Tolerations
core_concepts.definition: Allows Pods to run on tainted nodes.

comparisons.summary: DaemonSet focuses on nodes; Deployment focuses on application replicas.
DaemonSet follows node count; ReplicaSet follows replica count.

resolution_prevention.anti_pattern: Using DaemonSet for normal application scaling.

performance_considerations: One Pod per node increases resource usage

response: DaemonSet runs a copy of a Pod on each node.
It is commonly used for logging and monitoring agents.
interview_answer.why: Common cluster design question.

slides.interview_kill_shot: DaemonSet scales with nodes, not user traffic.

slides.definition: A Job creates Pods that run until a task completes successfully.
slides.why_it_matters: Jobs handle one-time tasks like migrations, backups, and batch processing.
slides.real_world_scenario: A database migration runs once during application deployment and exits after completion.

architecture_flow.diagram: Job → Pod → Process Complete → Job Success

comparisons.summary: Job finishes work; Deployment keeps application running.

response: Jobs manage workloads that should complete and stop.
interview_answer.why: Important for batch processing scenarios.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Deployment keeps Pods alive; Job expects Pods to finish.

slides.definition: CronJob creates Jobs on a scheduled time interval using cron syntax.
slides.why_it_matters: CronJobs automate recurring tasks inside Kubernetes.
slides.real_world_scenario: A backup task runs every night at 2 AM using a CronJob.

comparisons.summary: CronJob creates Jobs repeatedly; Job runs once.

response: CronJob automates recurring Jobs using schedules.
interview_answer.why: Common automation question.

slides.interview_kill_shot: CronJob schedules Jobs; it does not directly run containers.

slides.definition: A Namespace is a logical partition inside a Kubernetes cluster used to organize and isolate resources.
slides.why_it_matters: Namespaces allow teams, applications, and environments to share the same cluster safely.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company uses one cluster with separate namespaces for development, staging, and production workloads.

core_concepts.name: Logical Isolation
core_concepts.definition: Separates resources without creating multiple clusters.

comparisons.summary: Namespace is logical isolation; cluster is physical Kubernetes environment.
Namespace groups workloads; Node provides compute resources.

performance_considerations: Namespaces do not provide hard performance isolation

response: Namespaces provide logical isolation and organization inside a cluster.
They are commonly used for environments and teams.
interview_answer.why: Namespace design is important in enterprise clusters.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Namespaces isolate Kubernetes resources, not physical infrastructure.

slides.definition: Resource management controls how much CPU and memory Pods request and consume.
slides.why_it_matters: Proper resource settings prevent node overload, improve scheduling, and increase cluster stability.
slides.real_world_scenario: A service receives heavy traffic. Kubernetes schedules additional Pods because resource requests and limits are correctly defined.

architecture_flow.diagram: Pod Resources → Scheduler → Node Capacity → Container

core_concepts.name: CPU Request
core_concepts.definition: Minimum CPU guaranteed for a container.

core_concepts.name: QoS Class
core_concepts.definition: Quality of Service category assigned to Pods.

comparisons.summary: Request influences scheduling; limit restricts maximum usage.

response: Requests help scheduler place Pods.
Limits protect cluster resources.
interview_answer.why: Resource problems are common production issues.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Without requests and limits, Kubernetes cannot make intelligent scheduling decisions.

slides.definition: Kubernetes probes monitor application health and decide when containers should restart or receive traffic.
slides.why_it_matters: Health checks enable self-healing and prevent traffic from reaching unhealthy applications.
slides.real_world_scenario: An application starts slowly. Startup probe prevents Kubernetes from killing it before initialization completes.

core_concepts.name: Readiness Probe
core_concepts.definition: Checks if application can receive traffic.

comparisons.summary: Liveness restarts containers; readiness controls traffic.

response: Readiness controls traffic.
Liveness controls restart.
Startup protects slow applications.
interview_answer.why: Frequently asked reliability question.

slides.interview_kill_shot: A failed readiness probe does not restart the container.

slides.definition: Kubernetes scheduling decides which Worker Node should run a Pod based on resources, constraints, and policies.
slides.why_it_matters: Correct scheduling improves availability, performance, and workload distribution.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company runs GPU workloads only on GPU nodes and prevents normal workloads from consuming those resources.

architecture_flow.diagram: API Server → Scheduler → Node Selection → kubelet → Pod

core_concepts.name: Pod Anti-Affinity
core_concepts.definition: Prevents similar Pods from running together.

core_concepts.name: Tolerations
core_concepts.definition: Allows Pods to run on tainted nodes.

comparisons.summary: Affinity attracts Pods; taints repel Pods.
nodeSelector is simple; affinity provides advanced rules.

response: Scheduler selects nodes based on resources and constraints.
Affinity controls placement; taints control eligibility.
interview_answer.why: Scheduling questions test production knowledge.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Scheduler decides placement; kubelet only executes the assigned Pod.

slides.definition: Kubernetes networking enables communication between Pods, Services, Nodes, and external systems.
slides.why_it_matters: Networking failures are among the most common production Kubernetes issues.
slides.real_world_scenario: Frontend Pods communicate with backend Pods using Service DNS while NetworkPolicy controls allowed traffic.

architecture_flow.diagram: Pod → CNI → Service → kube-proxy → Destination Pod

comparisons.summary: Pod IP changes; Service IP remains stable.

response: Kubernetes networking gives every Pod an IP.
Services provide stable access.
interview_answer.why: Networking troubleshooting is heavily tested.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Pods communicate directly by IP, but Services provide stable discovery.

slides.definition: RBAC controls who can perform which actions on Kubernetes resources.
slides.why_it_matters: RBAC prevents unauthorized access and follows least privilege security principles.
slides.real_world_scenario: Developers can deploy applications but cannot modify cluster-wide settings.

comparisons.summary: Role is namespace-scoped; ClusterRole is cluster-scoped.

response: RBAC maps identities to permissions.
It controls Kubernetes API access.
interview_answer.why: Security is mandatory in production.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Authentication answers who you are; RBAC decides what you can do.

slides.definition: Kubernetes security features control container privileges and runtime behavior.
slides.why_it_matters: Secure workloads reduce attack surface and prevent container privilege escalation.
slides.real_world_scenario: A production application runs as a non-root user with restricted Linux capabilities.

core_concepts.name: runAsNonRoot
core_concepts.definition: Prevents containers from running as root.

response: SecurityContext defines runtime security settings.
interview_answer.why: Container security is common in DevOps interviews.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Running as root inside containers is a security risk.

slides.definition: Autoscaling automatically adjusts Pods or nodes based on workload demand.
slides.why_it_matters: Autoscaling maintains performance while optimizing infrastructure cost.
slides.real_world_scenario: An e-commerce application automatically increases replicas during peak traffic.

comparisons.summary: HPA changes replicas; VPA changes resources.

response: HPA scales workloads, VPA adjusts resources, Cluster Autoscaler manages nodes.
interview_answer.why: Scaling design is frequently discussed.

slides.interview_kill_shot: HPA scales Pods; Cluster Autoscaler scales machines.

slides.definition: Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes that simplifies application deployment using reusable templates called charts.
slides.why_it_matters: Helm standardizes deployments, reduces YAML duplication, and enables versioned application releases.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company deploys the same application across dev, staging, and production using different Helm values.

core_concepts.name: Chart
core_concepts.definition: Package containing Kubernetes templates and metadata.

core_concepts.name: Release
core_concepts.definition: Installed instance of a Helm chart.

comparisons.summary: kubectl deploys manifests; Helm manages versioned application packages.
Chart is the template; Release is the deployed instance.

security_considerations: Avoid storing secrets in values files

response: Helm packages Kubernetes resources into reusable charts.
It supports upgrades and rollbacks.
interview_answer.why: Helm is standard in production Kubernetes.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Helm manages releases, not just YAML templating.

slides.definition: Operators extend Kubernetes by introducing custom resources and controllers that automate application management.
slides.why_it_matters: Operators allow Kubernetes to manage complex systems like databases automatically.
slides.real_world_scenario: A database operator creates, scales, backs up, and repairs database clusters automatically.

core_concepts.name: CRD
core_concepts.definition: Custom Resource Definition adds new Kubernetes object types.

core_concepts.name: Reconciliation Loop
core_concepts.definition: Process of matching actual state with desired state.

comparisons.summary: Operator is a specialized controller with application knowledge.

response: Operators encode operational knowledge into Kubernetes controllers.
interview_answer.why: Important advanced Kubernetes topic.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Operators automate what humans normally do manually.

slides.definition: Observability provides visibility into Kubernetes workloads using logs, metrics, events, and traces.
slides.why_it_matters: Production systems require visibility to detect and resolve failures quickly.
slides.real_world_scenario: A team detects high latency using metrics, finds errors in logs, and traces the request flow.

comparisons.summary: Monitoring detects known issues; observability helps investigate unknown issues.

response: Observability uses logs, metrics, and traces to understand system behavior.
interview_answer.why: Production Kubernetes requires visibility.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Logs tell what happened; metrics tell how much; traces tell where.

slides.definition: Kubernetes troubleshooting identifies and fixes failures in Pods, Nodes, Networking, and Deployments.
slides.why_it_matters: Interviewers test practical production debugging skills.
slides.real_world_scenario: A deployment is failing. Engineer checks events, logs, resources, and networking step-by-step.

comparisons.summary: Logs show application errors; describe shows Kubernetes events.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Always check events before guessing.

slides.definition: Backup and disaster recovery processes protect Kubernetes cluster state and application data.
slides.why_it_matters: Failures can destroy cluster configuration and persistent data.
slides.real_world_scenario: An administrator restores cluster configuration after accidental deletion using an etcd backup.

comparisons.summary: Cluster backup restores Kubernetes state; application backup restores business data.

response: etcd stores cluster state and must be backed up.
Persistent volumes require separate backup strategy.
interview_answer.why: Recovery planning is important in production.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Without etcd backup, Kubernetes cluster state recovery is difficult.

slides.definition: Kubernetes maintenance involves safely upgrading clusters, replacing nodes, and managing workload disruption.
slides.why_it_matters: Production clusters need upgrades without causing application downtime.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company upgrades worker nodes one by one while applications continue running.

core_concepts.name: Drain
core_concepts.definition: Safely evicts Pods from a node.

comparisons.summary: Cordon stops new Pods; drain removes existing Pods.

response: Cordon prevents scheduling, drain safely removes workloads, and upgrades are performed gradually.
interview_answer.why: Production maintenance scenarios are common.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Drain respects workload movement; delete simply removes workloads.

slides.definition: kubectl is the command-line tool used to interact with the Kubernetes API Server.
slides.why_it_matters: kubectl is the primary tool for deploying, managing, and troubleshooting workloads.
slides.real_world_scenario: A DevOps engineer investigates a failed Pod using kubectl commands.

comparisons.summary: get gives summary; describe gives detailed events.

code_examples.title: Basic Commands
code_examples.snippet:
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod app
kubectl logs app

response: kubectl communicates with Kubernetes API and manages resources.
interview_answer.why: Almost every interview includes kubectl.

slides.interview_kill_shot: kubectl is a client; Kubernetes control plane performs the action.

slides.definition: Kubernetes manifests are YAML files that describe desired cluster resources.
slides.why_it_matters: Declarative configuration is the foundation of Kubernetes management.
slides.real_world_scenario: A developer commits Deployment and Service YAML files into Git and deploys through CI/CD.

comparisons.summary: Declarative defines desired state; imperative executes commands.

response: YAML describes the desired state of Kubernetes resources.
interview_answer.why: Manifest knowledge is required for DevOps roles.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Kubernetes continuously reconciles actual state with YAML desired state.

slides.definition: CI/CD integration automates building, testing, and deploying applications to Kubernetes.
slides.why_it_matters: Automation enables reliable and repeatable releases.
slides.real_world_scenario: Code merge triggers pipeline, builds image, pushes registry, and updates Kubernetes deployment.

core_concepts.name: GitOps
core_concepts.definition: Git as source of deployment truth.

comparisons.summary: CI/CD provides automation, consistency, and auditability.

response: CI/CD pipelines automate Kubernetes deployments using manifests or Helm.
interview_answer.why: Most Kubernetes roles involve delivery automation.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Kubernetes runs workloads; CI/CD decides when and how changes are delivered.

slides.definition: Managed Kubernetes services provide Kubernetes clusters where cloud providers manage control plane operations.
slides.why_it_matters: Most production Kubernetes deployments run on managed cloud platforms.
slides.real_world_scenario: A company runs applications on managed Kubernetes with cloud load balancers and managed storage.

architecture_flow.diagram: Cloud Provider → Managed Control Plane → Node Groups → Pods

core_concepts.name: Cloud Integration
core_concepts.definition: Integration with storage and networking services.

comparisons.summary: Managed services reduce operational overhead.

response: Managed Kubernetes provides hosted control planes with cloud integrations.
interview_answer.why: Cloud Kubernetes is common in industry.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Managed Kubernetes removes control-plane management, not Kubernetes concepts.

slides.definition: Scenario-based questions test the ability to diagnose Kubernetes issues and make production-level design decisions.
slides.why_it_matters: Interviewers evaluate practical Kubernetes understanding rather than only theoretical knowledge.
slides.real_world_scenario: A production application is unavailable. Engineer identifies whether the issue is with Pods, Nodes, Networking, Storage, or Configuration.

architecture_flow.diagram: Issue → kubectl Investigation → RCA → Resolution → Prevention

core_concepts.name: Pending Pod
core_concepts.definition: Pod is created but not scheduled.

comparisons.summary: Application issues appear in logs; Kubernetes issues appear in events and resource status.
Readiness removes traffic; liveness restarts container.
Deployment for stateless apps; StatefulSet for stable identity and storage.

code_examples.title: Production Debug Flow
code_examples.snippet:
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod>
kubectl get events

code_examples.title: Check Service Routing
code_examples.snippet:
kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpoints

investigation.expected_finding: Scheduling, image, probe, or volume errors

rca.root_cause: Configuration, resource, networking, or application issue

resolution_prevention.best_practice: Follow systematic troubleshooting instead of random changes.
resolution_prevention.anti_pattern: Deleting Pods without understanding the issue.

response: I start by checking Pod status, then describe events, then inspect logs.
After identifying the root cause, I apply the smallest safe fix and add prevention.
interview_answer.why: This demonstrates structured production troubleshooting.

slides.interview_kill_shot: Never start by restarting Pods. First identify why Kubernetes is failing.
common_interview_questions: Pod stuck in Pending. How will you debug?
Service is not reachable. What do you check?
How do you perform zero downtime deployment?

rapid_fire_qa.question: First command during troubleshooting?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: kubectl get pods and kubectl describe to understand the state.

rapid_fire_qa.question: Where does Kubernetes store cluster state?

follow_up_questions: How would you design highly available Kubernetes?
How do you secure a cluster?
How do you handle production deployments?

dynamic_cards.content: Restarting a Pod may temporarily hide the real issue.
Strong answers explain commands, reasoning, and prevention.
